title: Newton's Laws of Motion
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Newton's Laws of Motion Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Investigate Newton's laws of motion and quantitatively analyse the relationship between force, mass and acceleration of objects (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 10 science worksheets on Newton's laws of motion: inertia, net force, F = ma, weight and mass, acceleration, action–reaction pairs, and stopping distances and car safety. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: A net force makes an object accelerate; more mass needs more force for the same acceleration.
body_html:
How to think about it

Newton's three laws describe how forces change motion.

  • First law: without a net force, an object stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity (inertia).
  • Second law: F = ma. Weight W = mg, with g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth. Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time.
  • Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects.
Example

Net force 600 N on a 200 kg cart. Acceleration?

a = F ÷ m

600 ÷ 200

Answer: 3 m/s²

Example

A 60 kg student. Weight on Earth?

W = mg

60 × 9.8

Answer: 588 N

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a moving object needs a force to keep moving at constant speed.
  • Thinking action–reaction forces cancel (they act on different objects).
  • Mixing up mass (kg) and weight (N).

faq.q: Why don't action and reaction forces cancel?
faq.a: They act on different objects. Only forces acting on the same object can cancel each other.

faq.q: How do car safety features use Newton's laws?
faq.a: Seatbelts and airbags stop your body continuing forward (first law) and increase the stopping time, so the force on you is smaller (second law).
Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. Speed, tiredness, alcohol and phones increase reaction distance; wet roads and worn tyres increase braking distance.

items.q: What is inertia?
c: an object's resistance to a change in its motion

items.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
c: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the force of gravity on it.

items.q: What is resultant force?
c: the total of all forces acting on an object, including direction

c: The acceleration of an object is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass (F = ma).
Objects at rest stay at rest.

items.q: Why does a gun or cannon recoil?
c: The bullet or cannonball pushes back on it with an equal and opposite force.

items.q: Do action and reaction forces happen at the same time?

items.q: Noah's 50 kg mass weighs 490 N on Earth. What would it weigh on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg)?

items.q: Mia pulls a trolley with a force meter and doubles the force. The acceleration doubles. What does this support?
c: Newton's second law: acceleration is proportional to force

items.q: Why do air bags and crumple zones reduce injuries?
c: They make the stop take longer, so the force on the passenger is smaller.
